messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: avaan WARNING: covariance matrix of latent variables is not positive definite;
parts: How can I reduce the high correlations between them to solve the problem

Did you use the semTools::indProd() function to calculate product indicators?  Read the References listed on the help page; I think the residualizing option implies the nonlinear-term factors would be orthogonal to the lower-order factors, but I don't remember.  Orthogonality might also require estimating residual covariances among product indicators which shared the same lower-order indicator (I forget all the details of that approach, I read that article back in 2011).  I usually recommend the default (double-mean-centering) approach, but you have quadratic as well as interaction terms in your model, so it's pretty complex.  Consider also looking into the LMS estimation available in the nlsem package.

FYI, this is a warning, not an error.  Your model ran, and there is nothing surprising about multicollinearity among terms when some predictors are functions of other predictors.  If your nonlinear effects are not significant, you can remove them from the model to make it simpler, which would reduce the amount of multicollinearity simply by having fewer nonlinear terms.  

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.author: 5d4f9e7f97c21008
messages.subject: Re: avaan WARNING: covariance matrix of latent variables is not positive definite;
parts:
To add to what Terrence said. With residual centering (orthogonalizing) the latent interaction/non-linear factors are uncorrelated with any lower order terms (and I believe they should be uncorrelated with each other, but that depends on how things were residual centered). With double mean centering the latent interactions/non-linear terms should be allowed to covary with lower order terms and each other too. Based on the results above, I'd be really surprised if either of those approaches were used (and the first thing I'd do is take a look at the indProd function and use one of those two approaches. For complex models (at least models with 3-way interactions there's some evidence that residual centering provides less bias than double mean centering: https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0013164412445473 but that is under a case where assumptions for residual centering are met)

In terms of including residual covariances among the indicators, that depends on if you're using a matched pair strategy to create indicators or if you're creating all possible pairs of indicators. If you use a matched pair strategy, then there's no need for residual covariances, since there's no overlap among indicators of the latent interaction/non-linear variable, if you use all possible pairs of indicators then you need to include residual covariances (this is true whether you use double mean centering or residual centering).

Alex
